ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A system composed of two equal and opposite charges is called an electric dipole. They can perform circular motion around a certain point on their connecting line without attracting each other, treating each charge forming the electric dipole as a point charge.

1. If their masses are all $m$, charges are all $q$, and the distance between them is $a$. Find the kinetic energy of the system's motion.
2. Now, place the system in a uniform magnetic field with magnetic induction strength $B$, where the direction of the magnetic field is perpendicular to their plane of motion, as shown in the figure. After reaching a steady state, the distance between them is $b$. Find the period of motion of the system.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description first: The attached figure shows two point charges at the two ends of a horizontal line segment in a plane filled with “×” marks, so the uniform magnetic field is directed perpendicular to the plane, into the page. The charges form a horizontal dipole, with one charge labeled q and the other labeled −q, and the tangential velocity arrows at the two ends indicate opposite directions of motion about a point on their connecting line. Reasoning for part 1: With no magnetic field and equal masses, the rotation center is the midpoint of the two charges. Each charge moves in a circle of radius a/2. The Coulomb attraction between the two opposite charges has magnitude F = kq^2/a^2 and supplies the centripetal force for each charge, so kq^2/a^2 = m v^2/(a/2). Thus v^2 = kq^2/(2ma). The total kinetic energy of the two-charge system is K = 2·(1/2 m v^2) = m v^2 = kq^2/(2a). Reasoning for part 2: In the magnetic field, the rotation center can shift along the line joining the charges. Let the distances of +q and −q from the rotation center be r_+ and r_−, with r_+ + r_− = b. Let the common angular speed be ω. The Coulomb force magnitude is F_C = kq^2/b^2. From the field direction into the page and the indicated velocity sense, the magnetic force assists the inward Coulomb force for one charge and opposes it for the other. Thus, up to interchanging the two charge labels, mω^2 r_+ = kq^2/b^2 + qBω r_+, mω^2 r_− = kq^2/b^2 − qBω r_−. Rearranging gives (mω^2 − qBω)r_+ = kq^2/b^2, (mω^2 + qBω)r_− = kq^2/b^2. Therefore r_+ = (kq^2/b^2)/(mω^2 − qBω), r_− = (kq^2/b^2)/(mω^2 + qBω). Using r_+ + r_− = b, b = (kq^2/b^2)[1/(mω^2 − qBω) + 1/(mω^2 + qBω)]. Combining the fractions, b = (kq^2/b^2)·(2mω^2)/(m^2ω^4 − q^2B^2ω^2). Canceling ω^2 gives b(m^2ω^2 − q^2B^2) = 2mkq^2/b^2, so ω^2 = q^2B^2/m^2 + 2kq^2/(mb^3) = (q^2/m^2)(B^2 + 2km/b^3). Hence the period is T = 2π/ω = (2πm/q) sqrt(b^3/(2km + B^2b^3)).

The Coulomb attraction between the two opposite charges has magnitude F = kq^2/a^2 and supplies the centripetal force for each charge, so
kq^2/a^2 = m v^2/(a/2).
Thus v^2 = kq^2/(2ma). The total kinetic energy of the two-charge system is
K = 2·(1/2 m v^2) = m v^2 = kq^2/(2a).

Reasoning for part 2: In the magnetic field, the rotation center can shift along the line joining the charges. Let the distances of +q and −q from the rotation center be r_+ and r_−, with r_+ + r_− = b. Let the common angular speed be ω. The Coulomb force magnitude is F_C = kq^2/b^2. From the field direction into the page and the indicated velocity sense, the magnetic force assists the inward Coulomb force for one charge and opposes it for the other. Thus, up to interchanging the two charge labels,
mω^2 r_+ = kq^2/b^2 + qBω r_+,
mω^2 r_− = kq^2/b^2 − qBω r_−.
Rearranging gives
(mω^2 − qBω)r_+ = kq^2/b^2,
(mω^2 + qBω)r_− = kq^2/b^2.
Therefore
r_+ = (kq^2/b^2)/(mω^2 − qBω),
r_− = (kq^2/b^2)/(mω^2 + qBω).
Using r_+ + r_− = b,
b = (kq^2/b^2)[1/(mω^2 − qBω) + 1/(mω^2 + qBω)].
Combining the fractions,
b = (kq^2/b^2)·(2mω^2)/(m^2ω^4 − q^2B^2ω^2).
Canceling ω^2 gives
b(m^2ω^2 − q^2B^2) = 2mkq^2/b^2,
so
ω^2 = q^2B^2/m^2 + 2kq^2/(mb^3) = (q^2/m^2)(B^2 + 2km/b^3).
Hence the period is
T = 2π/ω = (2πm/q) sqrt(b^3/(2km + B^2b^3)).
